Injury Analysis of Six NFL Players | Could they Make or Break Your Fantasy Draft?

by Maddox McCloud · September 2, 2026 · Featured

“It’s better to be lucky than good.”

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 15:18
Instaread

Those words, famously attributed to former New York Yankees pitcher Lefty Gomez, ring especially true in fantasy football. Injuries are an unavoidable part of the game, and sometimes the difference between a championship season and a disappointing one comes down to nothing more than being on the right side of the injury bug.

Luck isn’t the only factor fantasy managers can rely on when it comes to injuries. Understanding the injury itself, the player’s recovery timeline, and how it can affect their ability to perform on the field can help turn uncertainty into an advantage.

As a physical therapist, I have a different perspective when evaluating injured players. Rather than simply asking, “Will this player be healthy enough to play?” I want to know, “Will this player be capable of performing consistently at the level fantasy managers are expecting?”

With that in mind, I’ve identified three injured players I’m willing to target at their current draft price, as well as three others that I am avoiding because I believe their injury risk is being overlooked.

Tough Break, or Let it Ride?

Ashton Jeanty | RB, Las Vegas Raiders

It looked bad. Really bad.

On August 23, Ashton Jeanty went down during Raiders practice after landing awkwardly on his right leg. He couldn’t put weight on it and needed help getting off the field. His teammates eventually gathered around him in a prayer circle, a scene that immediately had fantasy managers fearing the worst.

However, the initial visual of an injury doesn’t always tell the whole story.

Jeanty was ultimately diagnosed with an ankle sprain, and subsequent reports indicated that the injury was not expected to be long-term.

Should fantasy managers be worried?

From an injury perspective, this is where things get interesting. An ankle sprain can range from a relatively minor injury causing a short-term limitation to a more significant injury that can affect an athlete’s ability to cut, accelerate, decelerate, and absorb contact.

Ankle sprains involve injury to the ligaments of the ankle. Ligaments are bands of tissue that connect bone to bone and provide stability to a joint. Ankle sprains are generally classified into three grades:

Grade 1: Mild stretching or microscopic tearing of those ligaments. Usually associated with mild swelling and pain, with little to no instability. Athletes can often return relatively quickly.

Grade 2: Partial tearing of a ligament, typically causing more swelling, pain, and some degree of instability. Recovery can take several weeks depending on the athlete and the specific ligament involved.

Grade 3: Complete tearing of a ligament with significant instability and loss of function. This is the most severe grade and generally requires a much longer rehabilitation process and, at times, surgical intervention.

Available reporting suggests Jeanty’s ankle sprain was relatively minor, with the running back already working with trainers and, based on reports, not requiring an ankle boot or crutches. While those details don’t definitively determine the severity of an ankle sprain, they are encouraging signs when evaluating a short-term outlook.

For a running back like Jeanty, those distinctions matter. It’s not enough for him to simply be able to jog in a straight line. He needs to plant his foot, change direction violently, absorb contact, and explode through holes without hesitation.

I am still willing to target Jeanty. The question for me is whether the injury has created enough uncertainty to push his draft price below his true value. If the market discounts Jeanty because of an ankle sprain that appears relatively minor, I’m willing to take advantage of it.

Doctors’ orders: TARGET

Jeremiyah Love | RB, Arizona Cardinals

Not all ankle sprains are created equal

Jeremiyah Love entered the 2026 season as one of the most exciting young running backs in fantasy football. After suffering a high ankle sprain, though, his status for Week 1 has become a legitimate question mark.

First, it’s important to understand how a high ankle sprain differs from a typical ankle sprain.

A high ankle sprain involves the syndesmosis, a group of ligaments that connect and stabilize the tibia and fibula— the two bones of the lower leg. Unlike a traditional ankle sprain, which commonly affects the ligaments on the outside of the ankle, a high ankle sprain occurs higher up and can be particularly painful with weight-bearing and twisting movements. For a running back, that’s a problem.

Every time Love plants his foot, accelerates through a hole, changes direction, decelerates, or absorbs contact from a defender, the structures involved in a high ankle sprain are being challenged. These aren’t movements Love can simply avoid while playing running back, and that’s where my concern begins.

Reports indicate the Cardinals have been cautious with Love’s recovery, with his Week 1 availability remaining uncertain. Even if he is ultimately cleared to play, being active doesn’t necessarily mean he’ll be operating at 100%.

From a physical therapy perspective, I care about more than whether a player can get onto the field. I want to know whether he can perform the high-level movements his position demands without pain, compensation, or hesitation. Even if Love plays, another potential issue is the workload. The Cardinals have little incentive to give their rookie running back a full workload if he’s returning from a high ankle sprain without a normal preparation leading into the season.

We also can’t ignore the Cardinals’ investment in Tyler Allgeier, who has already shown he can be a capable NFL running back when called upon. A reduced snap count or limited number of touches for Love could significantly lower his fantasy ceiling. He doesn’t necessarily have to miss games for Allgeier to become a problem.

That’s especially important when considering Love’s draft price (real-time ADP pick 3.05).

I’m not saying Love can’t have a great season. The talent is still there. The draft capital is still there. The opportunity is still there, but fantasy football is about value, and I’m not interested in paying full price for a player whose Week 1 availability and potential workload are both question marks.

The risk isn’t necessarily that Love will miss half the season. The risk is that fantasy managers draft him expecting the explosive, every-down back they envisioned and instead get a player who either misses the opener or spends the first few weeks working his way back to full strength. That’s why I’m avoiding Love at his current price.

If his ADP falls significantly, I’ll reconsider. Until we see him return to practice and demonstrate that he can handle the tools required of an NFL running back, there are too many unanswered questions for me to invest at his current cost.

Doctors’ orders: AVOID

Emeka Egbuka | WR, Tampa Bay Buccaneers

For a wide receiver, the big toe is more important than you might think

Emeka Egbuka‘s toe injury might not sound particularly concerning at first glance. After all, it’s not a knee, hamstring, or ankle. The big toe, however, plays an important role in one of the most important things a wide receiver needs to do: explode.

Egbuka has been dealing with a toe injury described as turf toe. Turf toe involves the first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint, located at the base of the big toe, and can occur when the toe is forced upward while an athlete is pushing off the ground. For a wide receiver, that’s concerning.

Every time Egbuka accelerates, breaks into a route, changes direction, or decelerates, he relies on his foot and big toe to generate and transfer force. He doesn’t need to be unable to walk for this injury to affect his fantasy production. He needs to be able to explosively push off that toe over and over again. The good news is that the available reporting has been encouraging, with Egbuka continuing to work through the injury without indications of a major structural problem.

From a physical therapy perspective, I care less about the injury label and more about function. Can he accelerate? Can he cut? Is he able to decelerate? Can he repeatedly perform those movements without significant pain or limitation?

If the answer is yes, I’m willing to take the risk and target the wideout from Ohio State.

If the injury causes even a modest drop in ADP, I think that could create an opportunity for fantasy managers. The talent and opportunity remain intact, and there’s currently not enough evidence for me to believe this injury will significantly limit his production.

The big toe may be small, but its role in a wide receiver’s game is anything but.

Doctors’ orders: TARGET

Malik Nabers | WR, New York Giants

An ACL tear can heal. Can Malik Nabers still be the same version of himself?

Malik Nabers suffered a torn ACL and meniscus last season, ending what was looking to be a promising year for the young receiver. After undergoing additional surgery this offseason, he’s now working his way back with the goal of returning for Week 1. For fantasy managers, the bigger question is not simply whether Nabers will play. It’s whether he’ll be the same explosive player he was before the injury.

ACL reconstruction can restore knee stability, but returning to peak performance takes more than medical clearance. Nabers still needs to accelerate, decelerate, cut, and change direction at an elite level.

Meniscal involvement adds another layer to recovery. The classic “unhappy triad” involves an ACL tear, MCL injury, and meniscus damage. While Nabers’ reported injury doesn’t necessarily qualify as the full unhappy triad, having multiple structures involved makes his recovery more complex than simply an isolated ACL tear.

That’s where my concern comes in. Nabers could be healthy enough to play while still lacking some of the explosiveness that made him such a dangerous fantasy asset. He could also have his workload managed early in the season.

Return to play doesn’t always equal return to performance. I’m also not willing to completely dismiss the fact that Nabers has already required additional surgery during his recovery. That doesn’t mean he won’t eventually return to form, but it adds another layer of uncertainty to a player whose fantasy value depends heavily on elite athleticism.

I’m not saying he cannot have a great season. He absolutely can. At his current draft price (real-time ADP 27.6, WR12), I’m not comfortable paying for the pre-injury version of Nabers while questions remain about how quickly he’ll regain his explosiveness. If his ADP drops enough to compensate for the risk, I’ll reconsider. Until then, let another fantasy manager take the risk.

Doctors’ orders: AVOID

Ja’Marr Chase | WR, Cincinnati Bengals

Sometimes the scary part of an injury is worse than the injury itself

Ja’Marr Chase hyperextended his left knee during practice on August 25, creating an immediate scare for fantasy managers. Chase was able to walk away from the injury, later describing it as a “little hyperextension,” and the Bengals have remained confident in his Week 1 availability. As of September 1, Chase is expected to be limited in practice this week, with head coach Zac Taylor saying he feels good about his progress.

From a physical therapy perspective, I want to monitor knee hyperextension, but the current information is encouraging.

The concern with a hyperextended knee is that the structures around the knee can be stressed when the joint moves beyond its normal range. Depending on the severity, this can lead to pain, swelling, ligament injury, or bone bruising.

For a wide receiver, I’m most interested in whether the knee can tolerate the actions taken on a play-to-play basis. So far, there aren’t many signs that Chase will be significantly limited in those areas. That’s important because Chase doesn’t need to slowly work his way back from a major reconstruction. He’s dealing with a relatively recent knee injury, but the team expects him to be ready for the season opener, and Chase himself has remained confident about his status.

I’m not letting this injury scare me away. At his current draft price (third overall), I’m willing to bet on the player rather than overreact to a minor injury scare. If anything, a small dip in ADP (Ed. note: Unlikely) would make me even more interested. Sometimes the best injury value is simply not overreacting.

Doctors’ orders: TARGET

George Kittle | TE, San Francisco 49ers

At some point, Father Time collects his payment

George Kittle is one of the most dominant tight ends of his generation. He’s also entering his age-32 season while attempting to return from a torn Achilles suffered in January. That combination is enough to make me (and most other fantasy managers) nervous.

The Achilles tendon plays a major role in generating and transferring force through the lower leg. It’s heavily involved in acceleration, jumping, sprinting, and pushing off the ground. For Kittle, that’s a dangerous proposition. His game has never been built around simply catching passes and falling down. He is an explosive athlete, a dangerous after-the-catch weapon, and one of the best blocking tight ends in football.

All of those responsibilities place significant demands on the lower extremity. While Kittle has made significant progress in his recovery, being cleared to play is not the same thing as being the same athlete. That’s especially important with an Achilles injury.

At 32, the physical demands of returning from an Achilles tear become even more significant. I’m not saying he can’t return to form. We’ve seen plenty of athletes successfully return from Achilles injuries; some multiple times.

Fantasy managers are being asked to draft Kittle based on the expectation that he’ll immediately return to being one of the most productive tight ends in football. That’s a bet I’m not comfortable making at his current price (real-time ADP in Round 6, TE9). There’s also the very real question of workload. Even if Kittle is active, the 49ers could manage his snaps early in the season as he continues rebuilding his strength and conditioning.

And then there’s the elephant — or perhaps electrical substation? — in the room.

San Francisco’s recent injury history has led to the infamous internet theory that the electrical substation next to the 49ers’ training facility is somehow responsible for the team’s injuries. No evidence supports that theory, but even Kittle has joked about wanting to make sure it isn’t an issue.

I’m not saying the substation is going to hurt Kittle’s fantasy value. I’m just saying I wouldn’t draft him and then start asking the 49ers where their nearest electrical grid is.

Jokes aside, the real concern is much simpler: Achilles recovery + age + elite athletic demands + premium draft price. Kittle still has massive upside if everything goes right.

When I’m drafting, I’d rather take a tight end with fewer questions surrounding his ability to regain his previous level of explosiveness. If Kittle’s ADP falls significantly, I’ll reconsider. At his current price, however, I’m letting someone else take the risk.

Doctors’ orders: AVOID

Maddox McCloud is the resident fantasy football injury analyst for PlayerProfiler.
